items.summary: You use your senses every minute of the day. After reading this, you can name the five senses, explain what each one does for you, and test your senses so you know how well they work.
items.title: Discovering the Five Senses

items.summary: Pip slips out of the gate and loses his way in the rain. Follow him from the first wet paw to the last step home. You will learn the three parts of a story, the words Pip's story uses, and the little trick that helped him find his own front door.
items.title: The Lost Puppy Finds His Way Home

items.summary: An always tells the truth, even when the truth is hard to say. Follow him through the day he breaks his mother's blue bowl. You will learn the three parts of the story, four new words, and what happened when he chose not to hide.
items.title: The Boy Who Always Told the Truth

items.summary: Fast mental arithmetic is a set of honest shortcuts, and every shortcut needs a check. After reading this article you can round and adjust a product, split a product into parts, work in tens, take a percentage as a fraction of ten, and subtract with a complement. You can also estimate an answer before you give it and check the answer in reverse.
items.title: Fast Mental Arithmetic You Can Check

items.summary: Trillions are invested, valuations soar, and every product announces intelligence. Is this the internet of 1995 or the tulips of 1637? This article examines how to think about AI hype: the difference between a bubble and a revolution, what real economic value looks like, and how inflated expectations can coexist with genuine technology.
items.title: AI Bubble or Real Revolution?

items.summary: Everything is getting easier — food arrives, entertainment never ends, answers are instant. This article asks what the removal of friction costs: patience, discipline, resilience and the ability to get through hard things, and how to keep the small doses of difficulty that a strong life needs.
items.title: The Paradox of Comfort: When Ease Makes Us Fragile

items.summary: Competence shaming is a way of gaining standing by lowering somebody else's competence, and the difference from honest criticism is the aim, not the words. After reading this you can name the four moves of the attack, tell honest criticism from a status attack, answer one without escalating it, and notice when you are doing it yourself.
items.title: Competence Shaming and Status Manipulation

items.summary: Gaslighting is the rewriting of a shared account until the person who was there doubts their own memory. After reading this you can tell a deliberate attack apart from an ordinary disagreement and an honest mistake, name the three moves of DARVO, recognise the pattern in plain language at work and at home, and answer it with sentences you can reuse.
items.title: Gaslighting and DARVO: Manipulating Perception and Turning the Blame Around

items.summary: Better tools produce better results — and the better results feel like better ability. This article examines the illusion of skill: borrowed competence, overconfidence after using powerful software, automation bias, and how to calibrate your real ability so your tools amplify it instead of replacing it.
items.title: The Illusion of Skill: When Powerful Tools Inflate Us

items.summary: Good and bad are not two materials inside a person. They are one capacity, used for two aims. After reading this you can name the five parts of an act, separate the capacity from the aim, explain why the same person can help or harm, read the six factors that turn a decision, and run a six-step check before you act at work, at home or in a meeting.
items.title: Angels and Demons Inside One Person: Good and Evil From One Source

items.summary: A grade, a certificate and a fast answer are proxies: cheap, standard stand-ins for ability. After reading this you can name what a score really measures, separate evidence from the conclusion drawn from it, compare six kinds of evidence from weak to strong, and use six steps to judge ability from real work instead of from a label.
items.title: The Illusion of Intelligence: When a Grade Is Mistaken for Ability

items.summary: Intelligence is not one number, and it is not the same as knowledge or skill. After reading this you can describe what intelligence is, explain why one mind is strong in one field and weak in another, separate the general factor from the specific profiles, and use six steps to write your own profile and put it to work in a team.
items.title: The Nature of Intelligence: Why One Mind Shines in One Field

items.summary: Knowing more facts does not make a person understand more. After reading this you can tell knowing from understanding, name the words that carry the difference, compare the two on six points, turn one fact into understanding with six steps, and ask the questions that make an answer usable at work.
items.title: The Paradox of Knowledge: Why Knowing More Is Not Understanding More

items.summary: Run a free model on your own machine, own the weights, keep your data — so you are independent now, right? This article examines the illusion of technological self-sufficiency: what local AI really frees you from, what it does not, and why the ecosystem underneath matters more than the model on your disk.
items.title: Free AI and the Illusion of Control

items.summary: An argument can be lost without a single false fact. When the ground moves — to the person, to the feeling, to a standard that changes after the facts arrive — the claim is never tested. After reading this you can name the nine moves, spot them in a live exchange, answer each one with one sentence, and keep your own argument clean when you are being pushed.
items.title: Psychological Manipulation in Arguments

items.summary: The most effective persuasion does not forbid opinions — it arranges the information environment so that some opinions arrive pre-made. This article examines how attention is steered in the digital age: agenda-setting, manufactured consent, soft power, self-censorship and crowd psychology, and how independent thought survives in managed information spaces.
items.title: Manufactured Consent: The Quiet End of Independent Thought

items.summary: Mathematics and literature are two machines for reaching a conclusion, and each one makes a different promise. After reading this you can describe how a proof is built and checked, explain how a story is judged, tell an error of deduction from an error of premise, and move between the two modes with six steps, from a certain fact to a sentence a person can act on.
items.title: Mathematics and Literature: Two Ways of Thinking

items.summary: Power is the ability to make things happen; authority is power the other side accepts. After reading this you can tell the two apart, name the five bases on which authority is claimed, test whether a decision can be questioned, and raise an objection in a meeting, in a review or in writing without turning the difference into insubordination.
items.title: Power Dynamics and Authority Manipulation

items.summary: A currency is a promise, a code and a habit. After reading this article you can tell the name of a currency from its ISO 4217 code and its symbol, explain why one currency serves many countries, read a note and name its denomination and its minor unit, describe how a market, a taxi or a restaurant expects payment, and say what money means in the culture you work in.
items.title: The Currencies of 195 Countries: How They Are Used and What Money Means

items.summary: Attachment styles describe the promises a person brings to a partner, the way they read availability, and what they do when a partner is unavailable. After reading this you can name the four styles, describe what each one looks for and fears, recognise the signals that switch your own pattern on, and say what you need in words your partner can act on.
items.title: Attachment Styles in Romantic Relationships

items.summary: Emotions do not decide what you say next, and relationships run on rules nobody writes down. After reading this you can tell the difference between regulating a feeling and hiding it, describe what a partner sees when a feeling is suppressed, reappraised or rehearsed, name the expectations under a conflict, and use short sentences to ask for a pause, state a need and agree a repair.
items.title: Emotional Regulation and Relationship Expectations

items.summary: An average difference between two groups says where the centres of two clouds sit, not where any one person stands. After reading this you can name the five parts of emotional maturity, say what a claim about men and women can and cannot tell you about one person, read a group claim without turning it into a rule, and hold a conversation about it without the argument becoming a fight.
items.title: Gender Differences in Emotional Maturity

items.summary: A gender role is a rule about what a category of people is expected to do. After reading this you can tell a role from a stereotype, name who enforces the rule around you, see how the cost of breaking it falls on one person, and negotiate a division of work at home or at work before the next crisis decides it for you.
items.title: Gender Roles and Social Expectations

items.summary: Loneliness is a feeling, and being alone is a fact, and the two are easily confused. After reading this you can tell loneliness, isolation, alienation and solitude apart, explain why a standard rises and what a closed door costs, describe commitment as a series of small decisions, and say what you want from a relationship in sentences you can use.
items.title: Loneliness, Selectivity and Commitment

items.summary: Long-term singleness has a vocabulary of its own, and much of the trouble around it comes from using the wrong word. After reading this you can tell the state of being single from the story a person tells about it, name the words that describe it precisely, recognise the pressure underneath it, and answer the questions other people ask without apologising for the answer.
items.title: The Psychology of Long-Term Singleness

items.summary: Marriage timing is not one decision but a set of forces: work, money, study, family, law and the people around you. After reading this you can name the forces that push a date earlier or later, use the vocabulary of timing accurately, tell the peer effect from the family effect, and run a short procedure that separates the practical questions from the pressure.
items.title: The Psychology of Marriage Timing

items.summary: Mate selection is the process of choosing a partner, and it has its own vocabulary. After reading this you can separate attraction, preference and decision, describe how people actually choose, read the direction and the size of an age gap, and run a short check on the preferences you say you hold.
items.title: Mate Selection and Age Preferences

items.summary: Short videos and infinite feeds are engineered to hold your attention, and the result is a tired, scattered feeling after hours of scrolling. After reading this you can tell the difference between a weak attention span and a strong habit, spot the signs that the feed has taken over your day, and run a one-week reset that gives you your focus back.
items.title: Brain Rot: Is the Internet Destroying Our Attention Span?

items.summary: A language model does not look up answers. It learns patterns from a large amount of text, and at run time it predicts the next token, one token at a time. After reading this you can explain how a model is trained, what the context window holds, why a fluent answer can be wrong, and what to check before you trust an output at work.
items.title: How AI Actually Works: Training, Prediction and Its Limits

items.summary: Artificial intelligence moved from research papers to daily tools in a few years, and it now touches your work, your phone and your money. After reading this you can explain what modern AI actually does, name the jobs it does well and badly, spot the three failure modes before you trust an answer, and decide what to hand over to a machine and what to keep.
items.title: The AI Revolution: How Smart Machines Are Changing Our Lives

items.summary: Scam messages are built on a small number of patterns, and those patterns leave signals you can learn to read in seconds. After reading this you can recognise the four structures behind almost every scam, spot the tells in a message before you act, run the first-ten-minutes procedure after an incident, choose payment methods that can be reversed, and say the sentences that stop a scammer without alarming the people around you.
items.title: How to Spot Online Scams and Fake Messages

items.summary: A chatbot does not read your message; it reads tokens, and the limits on how many tokens it can hold explain most of what feels strange about it. After reading this you can explain what a token is, judge whether a message will fit in the context window, count tokens roughly, write prompts that get better answers, and recognise the moment a long chat has stopped being reliable.
items.title: Understanding AI Tokens and How Chatbots Work

items.summary: An airport looks like one big building until you try to find a gate in it. After reading this you can read the signs, follow the process in the right order, transfer between flights without panic, and ask the right question when the plan breaks.
items.title: Navigating an Airport Without Getting Lost

items.summary: A hotel desk is a negotiation with rules you cannot see. After reading this you can read a booking, check in without queues, check the room in five minutes, ask for what you need, and leave without a surprise on the bill.
items.title: Checking Into a Hotel Like a Pro

items.summary: A menu in a language you do not read is a short problem with a known solution. After reading this you can read any menu, order exactly what you want, explain a dietary need, pay the right amount and tip in the local way.
items.title: Ordering Food in a Foreign Country

items.summary: Losing a passport is a bureaucratic problem, not a disaster, but only if you act in the right order. After reading this you can report the loss correctly, get the right documents from the right office, and travel home while you wait.
items.title: What to Do When You Lose Your Passport

items.summary: Persuasion is ordinary in a negotiation; the dark part is using it to hide the real price, the real stock or the real deadline. After reading this you can name nine techniques, say what the honest version of the same request is, and prepare the two things that protect you: your alternative and your walk-away price.
items.title: Dark Psychology in Business and Negotiation

items.summary: Professional email is a written register with its own rules: a subject line that gets opened, a structure the reader can scan, and a tone that survives being read without your voice. After reading this you can write a clear request, a careful apology, a firm refusal and a follow-up, and you will know the words each of them needs.
items.title: Writing Professional Emails in English

items.summary: Every workplace has a layer of language that is not in the dictionary: phrases for a meeting, a delay, a mistake, a decision. After reading this you will understand the expressions you hear in offices, use them at the right moment, and avoid the ones that make you sound either too casual or too managerial.
items.title: Understanding Common Workplace Expressions

items.summary: An interview introduction is not a biography. It is a short, structured answer that tells the interviewer who you are, why you are relevant and what you want next. After reading this you can prepare a 60-second introduction, describe your experience with evidence, ask questions that show judgement, and close the interview and follow up in a way that is remembered.
items.title: How to Introduce Yourself in a Job Interview
